title: Hallucinations, Misinformation and Deepfakes

thumbnail.headline: Confident, But Wrong

slide.title: Confident, But Wrong
slide.body: A chat bubble listing three tidy citation cards; the cards dissolve into dotted outlines with a small question mark. Small tag: AI Ethics, Bias and Safety · Lesson 4.

production_notes: [VERSION] Free access to Claude and ChatGPT, and whether the free versions can search the web, differ by plan and change often. The voiceover names the tools only as examples and makes no claim about search features; check the live tools before recording the exercise mention.

Aigerim Bekova and her farming cooperative in Kazakhstan are fictional. The wheat-yield number and the 'study' are never shown as real figures; any on-screen number must be a clearly invented placeholder labelled 'Hypothetical'.
Deepfake scenes use stock or slides only: never show a real public figure, a real voice or a manipulated image of a real person.
Scene 6 hero clip is 7 seconds and the scene is about 23 seconds: hold the clip, then continue on a soft blur behind the presenter.

Hook.voiceover: You ask a chatbot for three research articles on your topic. It gives you three titles, three author names and three publication years, all in perfect format. You search for them. None of them exists.

Explain.voiceover: To understand why, you need to know one thing about how chatbots work. A chatbot, such as Claude or ChatGPT, is built on a large language model. It writes by predicting the next likely words, based on patterns in the text it learned from. It does not simply look up facts in a database.

slide.title: How a chatbot writes
slide.body: Prompt → 'predict the next likely word' loop (word, word, word) → answer. Side note: patterns, not a fact database.

Explain.voiceover: So a chatbot can produce text that sounds right, but is wrong. This is called a hallucination. It is most common with exact numbers, dates and quotes, with sources, with local or specialist topics, and with very recent events. And it comes in the same confident voice as a correct answer.

slide.title: Where hallucinations hide
slide.body: Exact numbers, dates, quotes · Sources: articles, books, court cases, links · Local or specialist topics · Very recent events

Explain.voiceover: Misinformation is false or misleading information that spreads. AI adds to it in two ways. People copy hallucinated answers without checking. And AI can quickly produce large amounts of convincing false content.

slide.title: How AI adds to misinformation
slide.body: Left: copied answers (unchecked chatbot text pasted into a report). Right: mass production (many convincing fake posts appearing at once).

Explain.voiceover: Deepfakes are AI-made images, voices or videos that show people saying or doing things they never did. A fake voice message from a manager could ask for an urgent payment. A fake video could show a public figure making a false statement. Deepfakes make false stories look and sound real.
Explain.stock_query: worried person listening to phone voicemail

Explain.voiceover: Here is a simple way to think about it. A chatbot is like a very confident friend who has read a lot, but never checks notes. Most of the time their answers are helpful. Sometimes they fill a gap in their memory with something that sounds right, in exactly the same calm voice.
Explain.broll_prompt: Two friends in their thirties, a Latin American man and a Middle Eastern woman, chat at a small café table; the man speaks with easy confidence and open hands while the woman listens and quietly checks something on her phone; slow orbit from medium shot; warm late-afternoon window light; cinematic, natural colours, shallow depth of field; 7 seconds; no readable text, no logos.

Explain.voiceover: Three habits help. Check claims against a trusted source. Ask for sources, then open them. And slow down when content makes you feel a strong emotion, such as anger, fear or excitement. False content often tries to make you share or act fast.

slide.title: Three habits
slide.body: 1. Check against a trusted source · 2. Ask for sources, then open them · 3. Slow down when you feel a strong emotion

Demonstrate.voiceover: Let's see the habits in action. Aigerim Bekova writes a newsletter for a farming cooperative in Kazakhstan. She asks a chatbot for the average wheat yield in her region, and which study shows it. The chatbot gives a precise number and names a study.
Demonstrate.stock_query: woman writing newsletter laptop rural office

Demonstrate.voiceover: Aigerim follows the three habits. She checks the number on her country's official agriculture website, and the official figure is different. She searches for the study, and cannot find it. The source was invented. And she notices that the answer felt reliable only because it was so specific and confident.

slide.title: Checking the answer
slide.body: Chatbot answer: number + study (placeholder values, labelled Hypothetical) → Habit 1: official figure differs (red cross) → Habit 2: study not found (red cross) → Habit 3: confidence is not proof.

Demonstrate.voiceover: She uses the official figure, links to the official source, and adds one line to her team's guidance. Never publish a number or a source from a chatbot until you have opened the original. It is a small rule, but it protects the whole team.

slide.title: New team rule
slide.body: "Never publish a number or a source from a chatbot until you have opened the original."

Demonstrate.voiceover: The same week, a member forwards a voice message that claims to be from the director, asking for a quick payment to a new supplier. Aigerim calls the director on a known number. The director did not send it.
Demonstrate.stock_query: woman making phone call at office desk

Demonstrate.voiceover: A common mistake is to think that if a chatbot gives a source, the answer must be correct. A source only counts after you have opened it and found the claim in it yourself. A chatbot can also give a real source that does not say what it claims. And deepfakes are not always easy to spot, so check the context and confirm through a different channel.
Demonstrate.on_screen_text: A source counts only when opened

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, chatbots predict likely text, so they can produce confident answers that are false, including invented sources. This is a hallucination. Second, deepfakes are AI-made images, voices or videos that can make false stories look real. Third, check claims against a trusted source, open every source yourself, and slow down when content makes you feel a strong emotion.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Chatbots predict text: confident answers can be false. 2. Deepfakes make false stories look real. 3. Check, open sources, slow down.

CTA.voiceover: Now it is your turn. In the exercise below this video, you will ask a chatbot three factual questions about your own country or industry, check every answer against a trusted source, and record each error you find. It takes about twenty minutes. In the next lesson, we will look at privacy, and what happens to the data you share. See you there.
